lesson.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
lesson.summary: Introduces electromagnetic radiation as a continuum of waves ordered by wavelength and frequency, and shows how those two properties determine the energy a wave carries.
lesson.body:
You already know that energy is a quantity that can be transferred and transformed, but so far you've mostly thought about it in terms of moving objects or heat. Light is another carrier of energy, and it comes in a huge range of forms ,  radio waves, visible light, X-rays, and more ,  that are all fundamentally the same kind of thing: oscillating electric and magnetic fields traveling through space. The electromagnetic spectrum is simply the full range of these waves, arranged according to two properties that are locked together: wavelength (the distance between successive peaks of the wave) and frequency (how many wave cycles pass a point per second).

The reason wavelength and frequency are locked together is that every form of electromagnetic radiation travels through empty space at the same fixed speed, the speed of light, c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ meters per second. Speed, wavelength, and frequency are related by c = λν, where λ is wavelength and ν is frequency. Because c is constant, if you stretch out a wave to a longer wavelength, fewer cycles can pass a given point each second, so the frequency must drop; shrink the wavelength, and the frequency must rise to keep the product λν equal to the same constant c. This is why the spectrum can be laid out as one continuous ordering: at one end you have radio waves, with wavelengths of meters or more and very low frequencies, and as you move through microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and finally gamma rays, wavelength keeps shrinking while frequency keeps climbing.

What makes this matter for chemistry is that frequency determines how much energy a given "packet" of light ,  a photon ,  carries. This connects light directly to the energy concepts you already have, but with a new rule: the energy of a photon is E = hν, where h is Planck's constant, 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds. Because higher frequency means more energy, and higher frequency also means shorter wavelength, you can state the whole spectrum's energy ordering in one sentence: short-wavelength, high-frequency radiation (like X-rays and gamma rays) carries much more energy per photon than long-wavelength, low-frequency radiation (like radio waves).

You can see this concretely with a photon of green light, wavelength about 500 nanometers (5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m). Its frequency is ν = c/λ = (3.00 × 10⁸ m/s)/(5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 6.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz ,  six hundred trillion cycles every second. The energy of one such photon is E = hν = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)(6.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz) ≈ 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ joules. That is an almost unimaginably small amount of energy for a single photon, which is exactly why you never notice individual photons in daily life ,  visible light around you consists of enormous numbers of them arriving together. But compare a gamma ray with a wavelength thousands of times shorter: its frequency, and therefore its energy per photon, is thousands of times larger, which is part of why gamma radiation can damage matter that visible light cannot touch.

Keep this wavelength-frequency-energy relationship in mind as a single package: knowing any one of the three (λ, ν, or E) lets you calculate the other two, because they are never independent ,  they are three ways of describing the same electromagnetic wave.
